abstract: Speech-in-noise difficulties often exceed audiometric profile-based predictions, suggesting suprathreshold neural coding deficits limit understanding even when audibility is preserved. A major limitation of clinical speech tests is that reduced performance can reflect either hair-cell loss or cochlear neural degeneration (CND). We propose a computational framework estimating each factor relative contribution at a population level. We simulated auditory-nerve responses to a consonant-identification task for 94 adults (19-83 years; pure-tone average (PTA) 0-55 dB HL) under three conditions: audiometric loss alone, CND affecting low- and medium-spontaneous-rate (LS and MS) fibers, and CND affecting all fiber types. A convolutional autoencoder was used to learn low-dimensional embeddings from neurograms, and downstream classifiers were used to perform consonant identification from the embeddings. We found that audiometric loss alone, and CND of LS and MS fibers consistently produced mismatch between model and human accuracies, whereas CND affecting all fiber types predicted human accuracy closely (mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.089, r = 0.81, rho = 0.83) on an individual level, while capturing the broad structure of human confusions.
